Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson broke with her fellow justices Thursday regarding a fight over student ID and the midterm elections.
Fox News reported Friday that Jackson was the only justice to publicly dissent while other justices may have done the same but chose not to be identified on the court order.
The outlet said she stood alone against the court’s decision “allowing New Hampshire to block the use of student ID cards in the upcoming midterm elections.”

Other justices on the court cited the longstanding precedent “that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election,” and said that lower courts failed to argue that the specific case in New Hampshire warranted an exception to the tradition. Jackson, however, argued the proximity to an election should not get in the way of properly applying the law.
“I respectfully dissent because — even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming — I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes,” she wrote.
State law currently bars the use of student IDs as a person’s main form of identification, UPI reported Thursday after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled against their use for the midterms in New Hampshire.
“In a brief court order, the justices granted an emergency request by the state, which was backed by the Republican National Committee,” the outlet said.

sources.news_title: Justice Jackson Dissents on NH Student Voter ID Ban
sources.text:
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson again stood alone Thursday as the Supreme Court let New Hampshire bar student IDs for midterm voting, siding with election rules Republicans backed.
The high court cleared New Hampshire to keep student identification cards off the accepted list for voters requesting a ballot in the upcoming midterms. Fox News reported that Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to dissent in public.
A New Hampshire law signed in April and effective in June struck student IDs from the forms election officials can take when someone asks for a ballot. Secretary of State David Scanlan then issued guidance that went further. Student IDs could not establish voter identity even as supporting evidence under the state’s alternative verification procedures.
A district judge blocked that part of Scanlan’s guidance. The judge said it went beyond the law itself. The Supreme Court decision left the block on student IDs in place for the midterms.
The Republican National Committee backed the secretary of state’s guidance. A voting rights group sued New Hampshire, arguing the law illegally discriminated against young voters by making it harder for them to cast ballots. Students who once relied on campus IDs will now need another accepted form of identification. How many voters that touches remains unclear.
The other justices pointed to longstanding precedent. Lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter election rules on the eve of an election. They said the lower courts failed to show that this New Hampshire dispute warranted an exception to that tradition.
Jackson saw it differently. She wrote that proximity to Election Day should not stop the court from applying the law correctly.
In her dissent, Jackson stated:
"I respectfully dissent because, even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming, I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes,"
That stance put her out front of the rest of the bench again. The court has drawn similar bright lines in other recent fights over institutional authority and federal power, including when the Supreme Court let the Pentagon scrap deals that had spared alleged 9/11 plotters from death row.
Jackson has served roughly four years on the Supreme Court. She has already stood alone more than once. In 2023 she was the lone dissenter in an 8-1 ruling that allowed a concrete company to sue striking union workers. In May 2026 she again stood alone in a decision involving federal prisoners seeking to challenge convictions through compassionate release.
Those solo positions fit a broader record of sharp divides on the current court. Separate cases have produced clear majorities in other Trump-era policy fights, including a 7-2 win for the Trump administration in an FCC political ad dispute.
New Hampshire heads into the midterms with several close races. Fox News power rankings rate the Senate contest as leaning Democratic and the governor’s race as likely to go Republican. The student ID rule now sits in place for Election Day.
Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico has pushed to let voters use student IDs in his own state. The New Hampshire fight shows how that argument collides with state laws that tighten what counts at the polls.
The sequence was straightforward. Lawmakers removed student IDs from the accepted list. The secretary of state told local officials those cards could not even back up identity under backup procedures. A district judge tried to roll part of that guidance back. The Supreme Court refused to let the last-minute court order stick for the midterms.
Other recent Supreme Court matters have likewise tested how far lower courts and agencies can push against settled rules. The court has declined some Trump administration requests, as when it refused a bid to stop transgender surgeries for federal inmates, while granting others that preserved executive and state authority.
Here the majority treated the eve-of-election principle as the controlling guide. Jackson would have kept the district judge’s order in force so the public would receive what she called accurate information about the state’s processes. The rest of the court left New Hampshire’s tighter ID list intact.
Voter identification requirements remain a basic safeguard. States set the documents their election workers may accept. When a campus ID drops off that list, voters still have driver’s licenses, passports, and other standard forms. The alternative is a system that treats every last-minute lawsuit as a reason to rewrite the rules after candidates have already filed and ballots are being prepared.
Court watchers also track personnel questions on the bench. Public discussion of possible retirements has already drawn comment from President Trump, who praised Justice Alito after reports on a possible retirement.
For now the operative fact in New Hampshire is simple. Student IDs will not get a voter a ballot in the midterms. The secretary of state’s guidance, backed by the RNC and left standing by the Supreme Court, sets the terms. Jackson’s dissent is on the record. The majority held the line.
Common-sense ID rules protect lawful voters. Courts that refuse to rewrite them days before an election do the same.

A late election fight has produced an intervention from the Supreme Court, with immediate consequences for identification rules.
At issue is how far federal judges should go when voting approaches and state officials are already implementing election procedures.
The Supreme Court allowed New Hampshire to enforce guidance excluding student IDs as evidence of voter identity Thursday.
The order delivers a victory to state officials and Republicans who supported their request for emergency relief.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented, challenging the majority’s application of the principle against judicial changes close to elections.
The case, Scanlan v. Coalition for Open Democracy, involves Secretary of State David Scanlan and a dispute over identification guidance.
New Hampshire’s legislature passed HB 323 this year, removing student identification cards from the list of expressly accepted voting IDs.
But the litigation reached beyond whether those cards could independently satisfy the state’s identification requirements.
It concerned whether election officials could consider them alongside other evidence through an alternative identity-verification process.
That distinction became central after Scanlan issued guidance treating student cards as unavailable for establishing identity under that process.
A federal district court left the underlying statutory restriction standing while ordering changes to the state’s guidance.
The Supreme Court stayed the district court’s October 2 and October 5 preliminary injunction orders.
The justices relied on the principle associated with Purcell v. Gonzalez, which cautions against federal intervention shortly before elections.
The majority said the district court had identified nothing sufficient to justify departing from that principle here.
The ruling allows state officials to continue their approach while the litigation proceeds through the appeals process.
For Republicans defending identification safeguards, the result preserves enforcement during the final stretch before the November election.
The Republican National Committee supported New Hampshire’s position, according to the Associated Press.
State Representative Donald McFarlane, the bill’s sponsor, welcomed the decision as a win for consistent identification standards.
“Today’s Supreme Court decision is a victory for common sense,” McFarlane said in a statement reported by the Associated Press.
He argued that colleges lack the same controls used by government agencies when issuing identification cards.
Jackson viewed the lower court’s intervention differently, arguing it addressed misleading explanations of existing law.
In her account, the district judge required accurate public information while leaving the state’s election rule untouched.
She reasoned that correcting inaccurate guidance could reduce confusion, serving the very purpose underlying Purcell.
The disagreement therefore involved both election timing and the characterization of what the lower court had ordered.
The district court examined a statutory provision permitting other evidence that reasonably establishes a prospective voter’s identity.
That provision supplied the basis for considering student cards within a broader assessment, rather than treating them as automatically sufficient.
The lower court found the state’s categorical guidance inconsistent with the remaining alternative verification provisions.
Its analysis distinguished removal from an approved list from exclusion as evidence in every relevant circumstance.
The state challenged the resulting injunction, bringing the timing question before the Supreme Court less than two weeks before voting.
Thursday’s intervention resolves which orders control immediately, while leaving the broader legal dispute subject to further proceedings.
The stay remains tied to the First Circuit appeal and any timely request for Supreme Court review.
If the Supreme Court declines that later review, its order provides that the stay terminates automatically.
If review is granted, the stay continues until the Court sends down its judgment.
Those conditions underscore that emergency relief and a final decision on the merits perform different functions.
The immediate enforcement victory does not amount to a comprehensive national ruling about student identification in every state.
Nor does the order establish that students are ineligible to vote simply because they attend college, The Associated Press reported.
The dispute concerns evidence used to verify identity, a narrower question than eligibility across the entire student population.

The U.S. Supreme Court has cleared the way for New Hampshire to enforce restrictions on student identification cards during the Nov. 3 elections, overturning a lower court order that permitted their use as supporting evidence of voter identity.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled Thursday, Oct. 22, that New Hampshire may prohibit voters from using student identification cards to establish their identity at polling places during the upcoming midterm elections, granting an emergency request from state officials less than two weeks before Election Day.
The decision temporarily blocks a federal district court order requiring election officials to consider student IDs alongside other evidence when voters lack an otherwise acceptable form of identification.
According to a Fox News Digital report published Friday, the justices based their decision on a longstanding legal principle discouraging federal courts from changing election procedures shortly before voters go to the polls.
The dispute centers on New Hampshire’s House Bill 323, which Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte signed into law in April. The legislation removed student identification cards from the list of documents expressly accepted for voter identification.
The law took effect June 2, after which Secretary of State David Scanlan issued guidance instructing election officials not to accept student IDs as proof of identity, including in circumstances where voters lacked other qualifying identification.
Voting rights advocates challenged that guidance, arguing that the secretary of state had gone beyond the restrictions authorized by the legislature.
On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante issued a partial preliminary injunction that left the statute in place but prohibited officials from categorically refusing to consider student IDs as supplemental evidence.
The judge distinguished between documents that automatically qualify as valid identification and other materials election officials may consider when verifying a voter’s identity.
Although House Bill 323 removed student IDs from the first category, Laplante found that the secretary of state’s directive improperly excluded them from the second.
The lower court concluded that the additional prohibition was likely inconsistent with constitutional protections and ordered state officials to revise their guidance before the November election.
New Hampshire appealed, arguing that changing the identification procedures so close to Election Day could confuse voters and election workers.
The Republican National Committee supported the state’s request for emergency relief.
In its Thursday order, the Supreme Court invoked the Purcell principle, which generally discourages federal judges from altering election rules immediately before an election.
The doctrine takes its name from a 2006 Supreme Court decision, Purcell v. Gonzalez, and reflects concerns that last-minute judicial intervention may create uncertainty about applicable voting requirements.
The justices found that the district court had not demonstrated sufficient justification for departing from that principle.
“Here, the District Court did not point to anything that would justify deviating from that principle,” the majority wrote.
The decision restores the state’s ability to enforce its existing restrictions while the legal challenge continues.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson publicly dissented, arguing that the lower court’s intervention was intended to prevent misleading information rather than create confusion.
“When a federal court determines that material misrepresentations are being made about a State’s election rules, an injunction to prohibit that conduct does not contribute to public confusion, it prevents that very problem,” Jackson wrote.
“I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes,” she added.
Jackson maintained that the district judge was responding to an executive directive that exceeded the limits of the statute itself.
New Hampshire Attorney General John Formella welcomed the Supreme Court’s decision, describing it as an affirmation of the state’s authority to administer its elections under established laws.
“New Hampshire has a responsibility to protect the integrity of its elections and ensure that election laws are applied as written,” Formella said.
“The Supreme Court’s decision is an important victory for our efforts to defend those laws and prevent last-minute court orders from creating uncertainty for voters and election officials. We will continue to defend New Hampshire’s election laws and the safeguards they provide,” he added.
Supporters of the restrictions argue that government-issued identification generally follows more consistent verification standards than identification produced by colleges and universities.
State Rep. Donald McFarlane, who sponsored the legislation, has defended the measure as a way to strengthen voter identification safeguards and public confidence in elections.
Opponents contend that students, particularly those attending college away from their permanent residences, may face additional obstacles if campus identification cards cannot be considered when verifying identity.
The dispute comes as New Hampshire prepares for a closely watched U.S. Senate election, increasing attention on voting procedures ahead of Nov. 3.
Under the state’s published Election Day voting requirements, registered voters must establish their identity to receive a ballot. The rules distinguish between identification accepted under the statute and alternative verification procedures for voters without qualifying documents.
The Supreme Court’s action does not eliminate those other procedures, but it permits officials to exclude student identification cards from consideration.
Importantly, Thursday’s decision does not resolve whether the challenged guidance is ultimately constitutional.
The justices addressed the timing of the lower court’s injunction rather than issuing a final ruling on the merits of the lawsuit.
The underlying litigation will continue, potentially allowing further consideration of the state’s identification requirements after the election.
For the Nov. 3 midterms, however, New Hampshire election officials may enforce the restrictions on student IDs, and voters who rely on campus identification will need to satisfy the state’s requirements through other permitted means.

The US Supreme Court on Thursday allowed New Hampshire to limit the use of student ID cards to serve as a valid form of ID to receive a ballot. New Hampshire’s HB 323, which went into effect in June, requires a government-issued ID to be presented to receive a ballot.
In an unsigned order, the court quoted the Purcell principle, from Purcell v. Gonzalez, which stated that “[c]ourt orders affecting elections, especially conflicting orders, can themselves result in voter confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls.” Purcell weighed the imminent election against the constitutionality of preliminary injunctions pausing voting regulations.
The United States District Court for the District of New Hampshire granted a partial preliminary injunction, noting that there is no likelihood that HB 323 is unconstitutional. However, it did find that a directive issued by the New Hampshire secretary is unlikely to pass constitutional scrutiny. The directive stated that student IDs could not be used for “any purpose at all.” However, New Hampshire Voting Requirements (RSA 654:12(d)(4)) allow “any other evidence that reasonably establishes that it is more likely than not that the person is who they claim to be.”
The Coalition of Open Democracy claims that HB 323 is unconstitutional because it infringes on young people’s right to vote in violation of the First and Fourteenth Amendments.
Following the district court’s ruling, New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan stated, “The court’s interpretation further creates a significant risk of unequal treatment of voters across the state because supervisors in each town and ward across the state will have to decide on a case-by-case basis whether a particular student identification card ‘along with other available evidence’ reasonably proves the voter’s identity.”

sources.news_title: SCOTUS Says NH Can Close Student ID 'Loophole' In Elections
sources.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court temporarily greenlit a New Hampshire directive on Thursday that prohibits the use and acceptance of student IDs in elections. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissent in the case.
In its new order, the high court granted an emergency application by New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan to temporarily pause a ruling by U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante. The Bush 43 appointee issued a preliminary injunction earlier this month blocking an April directive by Scanlan that said eligible voters can’t use student IDs as proof of identification when registering to vote, filing a request for an absentee ballot, or voting at a polling place.
According to local media, the secretary’s edict was issued to supplement a bill signed into law that same month by New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte that “made student IDs a no longer valid form of identification to obtain a ballot.” Bill co-sponsor and Republican State Rep. Ross Berry said the measure is necessary to ensure transparent and fair elections.
“Student IDs have no address verification,” Berry reportedly wrote at the time. “No citizenship check. No security features. They were the weakest link in our election integrity framework, and now that loophole is closed.”
Laplante’s injunction blocking Scanlan’s directive came at the request of several left-wing groups, including the state’s League of Women Voters chapter. The activist organizations claimed that the law is “unconstitutional and unnecessary.”
Scanlan filed an emergency request with the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals to pause Laplante’s order and permit his directive to take effect for the 2026 general election. The appellate court declined to do so (2-1) on Oct. 14, prompting the secretary to appeal to SCOTUS.
In its Thursday ruling, the Supreme Court cited the Purcell principle, which states that federal courts should avoid altering state election rules too close to an election. “Here,” the high court wrote, “the District Court did not point to anything that would justify deviating from that principle.”
In her dissent, Jackson argued that the order at issue in Scanlan “does not necessarily fall within the ambit of Purcell and its concern about federal courts ‘changing the election rules’ at the last minute.” She suggested that Laplante’s directive was not aimed at changing the law, but at “correcting a publicized misstatement about what New Hampshire’s election rules require was necessary to ensure that certain citizens were not unduly burdened in their exercise of the fundamental right to vote.”
“So [the district court] issued a targeted order, requiring only that the relevant government official conform his public statements to the letter of state law rather than summarizing what the law required in a manner that could mislead voters and local election workers,” Jackson wrote. “Consequently, here, the District Court’s injunction was reasonably designed to address alleged misinformation, not to change the law. Under such circumstances, the relief the District Court provided actually promoted the interests Purcell sought to protect.”
“I respectfully dissent because — even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming — I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes,” she added.
According to Thursday’s decision, Laplante’s blockade is “stayed pending the disposition of the appeal in the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit and disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari, if such a writ is timely sought.” The Supreme Court’s pause will terminate if a petition to SCOTUS is denied by the high court or if SCOTUS agrees to consider the matter and issue a judgment on the merits of the case.

Days later, the judge extended his order to cover public statements to that effect made by Scanlan. The injunction issued by the district court, Jackson said, “was reasonably designed to address alleged misinformation, not to change the law.”
“An injunction to prohibit that conduct does not contribute to public confusion, it prevents that very problem,” she said. “I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes.”
New Hampshire Attorney General John Formella hailed the Supreme Court’s ruling.
“New Hampshire has a responsibility to protect the integrity of its elections and ensure that election laws are applied as written,” he said in a statement.
“The Supreme Court’s decision is an important victory for our efforts to defend those laws and prevent last-minute court orders from creating uncertainty for voters and election officials.”
The Coalition for Open Democracy criticized the high court’s new ruling, calling it “wrong” and a misinterpretation of the Purcell principle.
“We applaud Justice Jackson for her dissent, in which she stands for the Constitution, the right to vote, and a rational application of Purcell,” the group said in a statement.
“We will continue to vigorously litigate this case in the defense of the fundamental right to vote of young voters across New Hampshire.”

The unsigned order was a win for New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, a Republican, and the Republican National Committee, which had supported Scanlan in the fight.
The court did not provide a vote count, though it did provide a brief explanation, invoking the “Purcell principle” that warns against last-minute decisions from courts that change election rules.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a liberal, wrote a dissent questioning the application of the Purcell doctrine in the case.
New Hampshire voters will fill an open Senate seat in November to replace the retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. A recent CNN poll found that Democrats enjoy a 31 percentage point advantage over Republicans among younger adults.
Lower federal courts allowed the state to enforce the central prohibition of a law enacted by the state legislature this spring. Under that law, student IDs on their own may no longer be used to verify a voter’s identity.
But the state law also includes a “safety valve” that allows voters to attempt to prove their identity through other means and the fight at the Supreme Court was about whether, in those circumstances, student IDs could be used as one factor, along with other evidence, to help officials identify people requesting a ballot.
New Hampshire officials interpreted the new state law as shutting off the ability to use student IDs even in those circumstances. A voting rights group called Coalition for Open Democracy sued. A federal district court blocked enforcement of that interpretation on October 2.
In her dissent, Jackson questioned whether it made sense to apply the Purcell doctrine to New Hampshire’s interpretation of the law. In this case, she said, the lower court didn’t change anything about the law the state enacted but rather only changed the state’s interpretation of the law.
“This so-called ‘Purcell principle’ arose in a particular context, and this court has yet to fully define its limits,” Jackson wrote, echoing a question about the doctrine’s lack of definition that critics have raised.
“I respectfully dissent because – even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming – I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a state’s electoral processes,” Jackson wrote.
Lawyers for the plaintiffs in the case criticized the ruling in a statement Thursday, saying it is “injecting confusion into the election—precisely what the Purcell principle is supposed to prevent—and authorizing an unconstitutional policy that will deprive young voters of their right to vote.”
CNN reached out to Scanlan’s office for comment.
The Supreme Court has been called on to address several high-profile election disputes heading into next month’s midterms, most notably a decision in mid-September rejecting President Donald Trump’s proposal to change how mail ballots are sent to voters across the country.
This story has been updated with additional details.

US Supreme Court says New Hampshire can reject student IDs as proper identification to vote
The U.S. Supreme Court issued an order Thursday that paves the way for New Hampshire to prohibit students from using student IDs to register to vote or obtain a ballot for the November election.
The backstory:
The state legislature passed House Bill 323 in April, which removed student IDs as a valid form of identification for students who wished to vote in the midterm election.
After the law went into effect, New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan issued guidance to election officials confirming the change and numerous trainings were held, according to New Hampshire Attorney General John Formella.
But a lawsuit filed by the Coalition for Open Democracy challenged the law and asked the courts to block it.
Part of the argument centered on the Purcell principle, based on a 2006 Supreme Court case, that established that last-minute court orders that changed election laws risked causing voter confusion and possible disenfranchisement as well as disruption for local election officials and their ability to properly administer the election. The case ended with in early October with the U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire issuing an injunction blocking that change. The state’s Department of Justice asked the nation’s highest court to block the injunction "to avoid confusion among voters and election officials alike," Formella’s office said in a release.
The Supreme Court granted the stay, meaning that the state can reject student IDs as a valid form of identification.
What they're saying:
"New Hampshire has a responsibility to protect the integrity of its elections and ensure that election laws are applied as written," Formella said in a statement. "The Supreme Court’s decision is an important victory for our efforts to defend those laws and prevent last-minute court orders from creating uncertainty for voters and election officials. We will continue to defend New Hampshire’s election laws and the safeguards they provide."
Part of the arguments involved the legal principle established in the case of Purcell v. Gonzales in 2006, in which the court argued that courts should not change election rules during the period just prior to an election because of the confusion it could cause.
U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson expressed her dissenting opinion with the court order, saying that the Purcell principle is meant to stop courts from rewriting election laws, but that in this case the lower court didn’t change the law; it kept the state statute intact and "only ordered the Secretary of State to fix misleading statements so they matched the actual written law." She also said ordering that state officials give accurate guidance reduces voter and poll-worker confusion rather than causing it.
She also argued that when a court acts to stop government officials from spreading inaccurate information about voting rules right before an election, higher courts shouldn’t step in to block that action.
In a statement, the counsel for the Coalition For Open Democracy called the high court’s order "wrong."
"The Court’s decision grants a stay which both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied, blocking an injunction that has now been in place for almost three weeks, injecting confusion into the election—precisely what the Purcell principle is supposed to prevent—and authorizing an unconstitutional policy that will deprive young voters of their right to vote," the statement read. "We applaud Justice Jackson for her dissent, in which she stands for the Constitution, the right to vote, and a rational application of Purcell. We will continue to vigorously litigate this case in the defense of the fundamental right to vote of young voters across New Hampshire."
What's next:
The Supreme Court’s stay means that New Hampshire election officials can refuse to accept student IDs. However, the stay is in effect until the lawsuit against the law itself is settled.
The New Hampshire Department of Justice will continue to defend the election law in the future court proceedings, Formella said.
The Source: Information in this story came from the New Hampshire Department of Justice, the U.S. Supreme Court website, the Coalition for Open Democracy and Ballotpedia. This story was reported from Orlando.

(The Daily Signal) – The Supreme Court in an 8-1 decision allowed New Hampshire to block student IDs as a valid form of voter identification.
In an unsigned order released Thursday, the justices paused Oct. 2 and Oct. 5 orders by U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante, a George W. Bush appointee, that prevented the state from enforcing its restrictions on student IDs.
Justices cited past precedent, noting, “This Court has repeatedly emphasized that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election.”
They added, “Here, the District Court did not point to anything that would justify deviating from that principle.”
In April, the state Legislature passed a bill, HB 323, to prevent student IDs from being used as valid identification to obtain a ballot. Lawmakers noted that student IDs often lack expiration dates and can remain in circulation after they are no longer valid, and generally lack the address verification, citizenship confirmation, and security features associated with government-issued identification.
The law went into effect in June. The Coalition for Open Democracy sued, alleging the law put an undue burden on the right to vote and discriminated against young voters.
Laplante’s order declined to block HB 323’s provision on student ID cards, SCOTUSblog reported. However, his ruling prevented the enforcement of Secretary of State David Scanlan’s April directive to local election officials extending that restriction to the law’s “safety-valve provision that permits a voter without qualifying photo identification to establish identity by other means.”
In his brief to the Supreme Court, Scanlan said election training on the new procedures had been underway for months.
“Over the next five months, local election officials were trained on the new identify-verification rules consistent with that guidance,” Scanlan’s petition said. “During that same timeframe, the secretary’s office published student voting guides, updated polling place posters, updated its website, conducted social media outreach, produced and ran radio ads, and spoke at public events to explain how identity verification would work.”
New Hampshire is among a few states that could decide which party controls the U.S. Senate, as Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas takes on former Republican Sen. John Sununu, the son of a former governor and brother of another former governor.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter Thursday, writing, “Consequently, here, the District Court’s injunction was reasonably designed to address alleged misinformation, not to change the law.”
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit had declined to pause Laplante’s ruling, so Scanlan appealed to the high court for the emergency ruling with days to go before the midterm election.
